source.ref: Regulation (EU) 2021/697, Article 2 (definition of 'legal entity') and Article 9(1)
source.text:
[Regulation (EU) 2021/697, Article 2, definition of 'legal entity'] ‘legal entity’ means a legal person created and recognised as such under Union, national or international law, which has legal personality and the capacity to act in its own name, exercise rights and be subject to obligations, or an entity which does not have legal personality as referred to in point (c) of Article 197(2) of the Financial Regulation;

[Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2018/1046 (the Financial Regulation that Regulation 2021/697 cites), Article 197(2)] 2. Any of the following applicants shall be eligible for participating in a call for proposals: (a) legal persons; (b) natural persons, in so far as this is required by the nature or characteristics of the action or the objective pursued by the applicant; (c) entities which do not have legal personality under the applicable national law, provided that their representatives have the capacity to undertake legal obligations on behalf of the entities and that the entities offer guarantees for the protection of the financial interests of the Union equivalent to those offered by legal persons.

texts.conditional: Your organisation is a natural person or has no legal personality. The regulation's definition names a legal person, or an entity without legal personality as in point (c) of the Financial Regulation, Article 197(2): its representatives can undertake legal obligations on its behalf and it offers guarantees for the protection of the Union's financial interests equivalent to those of a legal person. The call documents add, for natural persons: “Natural persons are NOT eligible (with the exception of self-employed persons, i.e. sole traders, where the company does not have legal personality separate from that of the natural person).” So a sole trader whose business has no legal personality separate from them may take part; any other natural person may not. The call and the Commission decide whether your case is accepted.

source.ref: Regulation (EU) 2025/2643, Article 11(7) and Article 2
source.text:
[Regulation (EU) 2025/2643, Article 11(7)] By way of derogation from paragraph 6, in order to take into account industrial cooperation with non-associated third countries, common procurement that involves a subcontractor that is allocated between 15 % and 35 % of the value of the contract, and that is not established or does not have its executive management structures in the Union or in an associated country, shall be eligible for support under the Programme provided that a direct contractual relationship related to the defence product has been established between the contractor and that subcontractor prior to the date of entry into force of this Regulation.

[Regulation (EU) 2025/2643, Article 2, definition of 'subcontractor'] ‘subcontractor’ means an economic operator that is proposed by a candidate, tenderer or contractor to perform specific tasks or services under the supervision of the main contractor, contributing to the design or manufacturing of a defence product, other than what is provided by suppliers to implement the contract, for which it is allocated at least 15 % of the value of the contract, and that needs access to classified information for the performance of that contract; for the purposes of this definition, ‘supplier’ shall be understood as an economic operator that delivers components of its own design or production to the contractor.

texts.info: Common procurement under the Programme can include a subcontractor that is allocated between 15 % and 35 % of the value of the contract and is not established, or has no executive management structures, in the Union or an associated country, if a direct contractual relationship related to the defence product was established between the contractor and that subcontractor before the Regulation entered into force (it was published on 29 December 2025 and entered into force on the following day). This figure is a share of the contract value. It is not the 35 % component cost limit.

[Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 (the Financial Regulation that Regulation 2025/2643 cites), Article 200(2)] 2. Any of the following applicants shall be eligible for participating in a call for proposals: (a) legal persons; (b) natural persons, in so far as this is required by the nature or characteristics of the action or the objective pursued by the applicant; (c) entities which do not have legal personality under the applicable national law, provided that their representatives have the capacity to undertake legal obligations on behalf of the entities and that the entities offer guarantees for the protection of the financial interests of the Union equivalent to those offered by legal persons.

texts.conditional: Your organisation is a natural person or has no legal personality. The regulation's definition names a legal person, or an entity without legal personality as in point (c) of the Financial Regulation, Article 200(2): its representatives can undertake legal obligations on its behalf and it offers guarantees for the protection of the Union's financial interests equivalent to those of a legal person. The call documents add, for natural persons: “Natural persons are NOT eligible (with the exception of self-employed persons, i.e. sole traders, where the company does not have legal personality separate from that of the natural person).” So a sole trader whose business has no legal personality separate from them may take part; any other natural person may not. REQ-AQAP2110.description:
AQAP 2110 Edition D Version 1 was promulgated by the NATO Standardization Office on 24 June 2016 and is still in force in 2026. AQAP 2210 (software quality requirements) is layered on AQAP 2110 or 2310 and is not standalone. AQAP 2120 no longer exists separately: it was folded into AQAP 2110 when Edition D was issued in 2016, so anyone still asking for AQAP 2120 is working from stale guidance.

Do you need it for EDF? Not to apply, but likely to deliver. No blanket AQAP requirement appears in the EDF, EDIP or SAFE regulations as an eligibility condition (those regulate control, establishment and component origin). It enters when a prime contractor or a national buyer names it in a contract, and it then cascades down to subcontractors.

Issued by national defence authorities (Government Quality Assurance) or by accredited certification bodies, depending on the country. Certificates run for three years with annual surveillance audits.

other_figures: Certification audit alone (stage 1 and 2): USD 4,000-10,000 (Ekontrol, vendor quote).
Polish certification body CertCom: from a few thousand to a few tens of thousands of złoty (vendor statement); the on-site audit takes one to several days.

REQ-EXPORT.description:
Two regimes are frequently confused. Dual-use items fall under Regulation (EU) 2021/821, whose Annex I is the control list. Military goods fall under the Common Military List, with transfers inside the EU governed by Directive 2009/43/EC and separate licences. A product can be in the military regime and not the dual-use one, so the first question is which regime applies.

The exporter is responsible for deciding whether its product matches an Annex I entry. Customs and tariff codes only signal that control is possible; they do not settle it. The basis is the manufacturer's datasheet and, where uncertain, a formal classification request to the competent authority.

This service asks which regime applies to your product and names the competent authority for the countries where we collected it (Spain, Germany and Poland). It does not tell you whether a given category needs a licence, it does not publish control list parameters or technical thresholds, and it gives no advice on controlled items.

REQ-FSC-ES.description:
In Spain the National Security Authority is the Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS), which works under the Secretaria de Estado Directora del CNI as the delegated authority for the security of classified information of NATO, the EU and ESA. The facility clearance is called HSEM (Habilitación de Seguridad de Empresa); the ONS maps it to the international Facility Security Clearance Information Sheet (FSCIS).

Related clearances: HSES (Habilitación de Seguridad de Establecimiento) is for storing classified material on your own premises and requires HSEM first; HPS (Habilitación Personal de Seguridad) is the individual clearance.

How long an HSEM takes was not published and needs a direct enquiry to the ONS. Other countries have their own National Security Authority; the research behind this page has collected only Spain's.

REQ-NCAGE.description:
The NATO Commercial and Government Entity (NCAGE) code is a five-character entity identifier. It is required for NATO Stock Number (NSN) assignment, for registration in NATO and national supply systems, and for procurement through NSPA. Holding an NCAGE code does not give any right to use NATO branding.

Who handles the request depends on the country. For NATO countries and a defined Tier 2 list, the request is handled by the national codification bureau (NCB); for everyone else NSPA handles it directly. The Tier 2 list includes Ukraine, alongside ARE, ARG, AUS, AUT, BRA, COL, GEO, IND, IDN, ISR, JOR, JPN, KOR, MYS, MAR, NZL, SRB, SGP and QAT.

The request starts in the NCAGE request tool: three mandatory fields on the first step (type of entity, other/priority, country), then a validation link is sent to the person who started it. Once validated, the priority cannot be changed.

REQ-SAFE-35.description:
The 35 % is measured against the estimated cost of the components of the end product. It is not measured against the contract value; briefings often paraphrase it wrongly as a share of contract value. There is also a separate, absolute prohibition: no component at all may be sourced from a third country that contravenes the security and defence interests of the Union and its Member States. The percentage allowance does not cover it.

The same Article also sets rules on establishment, executive management and control for contractors and subcontractors; they are listed on the SAFE card of the readiness page.
REQ-SAFE-35.name: SAFE origin rule (Article 16)

rules.note: The percentage is measured against the estimated cost of the components of the end product, not against the contract value. It is a property of the end product you would supply, so the answer is about one product.

source.ref: Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1106, Article 16(10), first sentence
source.text:
[Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1106, Article 16(10), first sentence] The cost of components originating outside the Union, EEA EFTA States and Ukraine shall not be higher than 35 % of the estimated cost of the components of the end product.

[Council Decision (EU) 2026/1381, recital (1)] was signed on 14 February 2026, subject to its conclusion at a later date, and has been applied on a provisional basis from 13 April 2026, pending its entry into force.

[Agreement between the European Union and Canada, OJ L 2026/445, Article 5(8), first sentence] The cost of components originating in Canada may exceed 35 % of the estimated cost of the components of the end product.

texts.conditional: More than 35 % of the estimated cost of the components comes from outside the Union, the EEA EFTA states and Ukraine. Canadian legal entities may take part in SAFE procurement under the agreement between the EU and Canada (Council Decision (EU) 2026/1381 approved it on 15 June 2026; the agreement is published as OJ L 2026/445). The decision says it has been applied provisionally from 13 April 2026, pending its entry into force, and we found no notice of its entry into force. For a Canadian legal entity the agreement lets components originating in Canada exceed 35 %, and sets other limits: at least 20 % of the component cost must originate in the Union, an EEA EFTA State or Ukraine, and the cost of components from third countries must not exceed the cost of those from the Union, an EEA EFTA State or Ukraine, and in any case 35 % (Article 5(8)). The answer you gave does not separate Canadian components from other third-country ones, so this is conditional.
texts.met: The share of components from outside the Union, the EEA EFTA states and Ukraine is within 35 % of the estimated cost of the components of the end product.
texts.not_met: More than 35 % of the estimated cost of the components of the end product comes from outside the Union, the EEA EFTA states and Ukraine.
texts.requires: The cost of components originating outside the Union, the EEA EFTA states and Ukraine may be at most 35 % of the estimated cost of the components of the end product.
texts.unknown: Give the share of the estimated cost of the components of your end product that originates outside the Union, the EEA EFTA states and Ukraine.
